title: Yaxel Lendeborg’s solution to career-worst shooting performance: ‘Go right to the barber’
content:
NEW ORLEANS — Yaxel Lendeborg wanted to make a change after playing the worst game of his life on Friday night. After going 1-for-13 from the field in a blowout loss to the San Antonio Spurs, the Golden State Warriors rookie admitted that he was mentally “cooked” and felt like he had let his team down.

In need of a transformation, Lendeborg looked for a new beginning the same way a lot of people do when they want a fresh start in life.

He got a haircut.

Gone are the wavy locks that became one of his trademarks as he rose to prominence as a national champion at Michigan. They have been replaced by a much shorter style, one so different that his own teammates had to do a double take during Sunday’s practice. While describing that he felt Lendeborg had responded “great” in practice after looking, and sounding, so dejected following Friday’s game, Kerr, who was standing just outside of the Hertz Center gym on the campus of Tulane University, where the Warriors were just wrapping up a workout, revealed the biggest surprise of the day.

“He chopped all his hair off,” Kerr said with a smile. “You’ll see. He got a haircut. I didn’t even recognize him. So, apparently that’s his response to getting beat by 100, is to go right to the barber.”

Kerr was referencing the fact that, during the outpouring of honesty at Friday’s postgame press conference, Lendeborg said the Warriors got “beat by 100.” But Kerr’s words Sunday revealed something deeper than the fact that the team’s star rookie had gotten a haircut. Kerr appreciated that Lendeborg was wearing his heart on his sleeve and used the rookie’s emotional honesty as a teaching moment for him and the team.

“Everyone sees the comments,” Kerr said. “I actually loved the comments. I don’t need false bravado. I need honesty, because you have to learn as a pro how to handle this stuff. And he’s learning so many lessons right now, and it’s our job to help him. But the lesson really should resonate with the entire team because that loss was on all of us. So we got destroyed. How are we gonna respond? That’s our challenge.”

Kerr said he spoke directly to Lendeborg on Sunday, but did so in the context of addressing the team as a whole. Kerr wanted Lendeborg to know he supported what he said, but he always wanted the rookie big man not to feel as if the weight of the world was on him in just his first month as an NBA player. Without Stephen Curry (torn oblique) on the floor, Lendeborg knows he has a lot more pressure to produce offensively each night. He failed to do so Friday, but Kerr doesn’t want that failure to carry over into Monday’s game against the New Orleans Pelicans and beyond. He wants Lendeborg and the rest of the group to be able to flush the poor performance and move forward.

“It’s not necessarily learning how to lose,” Kerr said. “It’s learning how to respond to a loss. So that’s the key.”

Specifically, Kerr was disappointed on Friday after feeling that his team didn’t remember specific details about the game plan. He didn’t disclose those details, but it didn’t matter. The Warriors got beat in every phase after having two separate film sessions and a shootaround to prepare for the game. Lendeborg said that he felt the team wasn’t aggressive enough and that the game would stick with him. That’s exactly what Kerr wants to try and change, but the 61-year-old knows from experience how tough that can be.

“It took me about 14 years,” Kerr said with a chuckle. “My last year, I finally was fine, but my first 14 years, I was a mess. I’m kind of kidding, but it’s one of the hardest things to do when you’re a competitor is to get over a bad loss and a bad personal game.”

Kerr’s secret to his success and his longevity as coach of the Warriors is his ability to connect with his players. He tries to find a way to meet each individual player wherever they’re at. He tries to pick them up when they’re down and keep them rolling when they’re up. Like everyone else, he sees the potential within Lendeborg. He appreciates Lendeborg’s approach to life, his happy-go-lucky style and the vulnerability he shows off the floor.

“There’s no pretense,” Kerr said. “He’s just telling you exactly how he feels.”

“He’s brutally honest,” Warriors guard Brandin Podziemski added. “I bet a bunch of people felt the same way. So like Steve said, it’s all about how we respond (Monday).”

Kerr just wants Lendeborg and the rest of his players to bounce back after a night like Friday instead of letting it linger. He wants them to learn.

“The message was for him, but also for the whole team,” Kerr said. “We lost by 100. We got destroyed. So, good teams learn by having a competitive response, and there’s details within that competitive response.”

Whether or not that response comes Monday remains to be seen, but for the time being, Lendeborg is doing what he can to make his own changes. Warriors guard LJ Cryer helped set up Lendeborg with a barber in New Orleans to make the new look happen. His new teammates and his coaches really like Lendeborg and believe better days are ahead for him. The new cut was just a step in the process. Podziemski understands. He cut off his own well-known locks prior to the season for a change of his own.

“New beginnings,” Podziemski said. “(Lendeborg) said he was gonna cut it like I did, so it’s pretty cool.”
